lede: Everything around you is built from atoms, and every atom is built from just three particles. Where those particles sit, what charge they carry and how the electrons are arranged explains almost everything else in chemistry: which ions elements form, and how they bond.
can: Give the charge, mass and position of protons, neutrons and electrons.
Work out the particles in any atom or ion from its numbers.
Write the electronic configuration of atoms and ions up to calcium.

md: An atom is far too small to see: hundreds of thousands of them would fit across the width of one hair. Yet chemists know exactly what is inside one. This lesson opens an atom up, counts what is in it, and shows why the way its electrons are arranged matters so much.

prompt: In the lithium atom above, where are the protons and the neutrons?
options: in the nucleus, at the centre of the atom
on the shells around the nucleus
spread evenly through the whole atom
answer: in the nucleus, at the centre of the atom
explain: Both are packed into the nucleus; only the electrons sit on the shells. In a written answer, name it: the nucleus. 'The centre' or 'the middle' on its own is not credited.

text: 1. Three particles, and what each one carries

md:
Every atom is built from **protons**, **neutrons** and **electrons**. Their charges and masses are **relative**, measured against the proton: a proton has charge **+1** and mass **1**, a neutron charge **0** and mass **1**, an electron charge **−1** and mass **1/1840**.
Keep the **+** on the proton's charge, and write the electron's mass as **1/1840**, not 'almost zero'.

title: Why the nucleus holds nearly all the mass
md: A proton or a neutron has about 1840 times the mass of an electron. However many electrons an atom has, they add almost nothing to its mass, so nearly all of it sits in the nucleus, even though the nucleus is tiny next to the whole atom.

prompt: Using the particle table above, why is nearly all of an atom's mass in its nucleus?
options: protons and neutrons each have a relative mass of 1, and an electron only 1/1840
the nucleus takes up most of the space in the atom
electrons have no mass at all
answer: protons and neutrons each have a relative mass of 1, and an electron only 1/1840
explain: The heavy particles are in the nucleus. The nucleus itself is tiny, not large, and electrons do have mass: just 1/1840 of a proton's.

md:
The **atomic number** is the number of **protons** in an atom. Protons only: bringing electrons or neutrons into the definition loses the mark.
The **mass number** counts the **protons and neutrons together**: the two added up, in one atom.
In an **atom** the number of electrons equals the number of protons, so the positive and negative charges cancel and the atom has **no overall charge**.

title: Where this mark goes
md: In Summer 2025 few candidates at either tier gave atomic number exactly. Many added electrons to the protons, some added neutrons, and every extra particle cost the mark.

prompt: Which of these is the definition of atomic number?
options: the number of protons in an atom
the number of protons and electrons in an atom
the number of protons and neutrons in one atom
answer: the number of protons in an atom
explain: Protons only. Protons and neutrons together is the mass number, and adding electrons is the slip the examiners penalised.

task: Put 3 protons and 4 neutrons in the nucleus and 3 electrons on the shells, and check that the net charge reads 0. Then take one electron away. Note what the charge becomes, and whether the element's name changes.

prompt: A lithium atom, with 3 protons and 3 electrons, loses one of its electrons. What is left?
options: a lithium ion with a 1+ charge
a lithium ion with a 1− charge
answer: a lithium ion with a 1+ charge
explain: The protons decide the element, and there are still 3, so it is still lithium. With 3 protons and only 2 electrons the charge is 3 − 2 = 1+.

md:
The Data Leaflet gives each element's **atomic number** (bottom) and **relative atomic mass** (top). For the elements up to calcium, except chlorine, the top number is the **mass number** of the common atom.
**The question.** How many protons, neutrons and electrons does an aluminium atom have? **[3]**
**Step 1 — protons.** The atomic number is 13, so **13 protons**.
**Step 2 — neutrons.** Mass number take away atomic number: 27 − 13 = **14 neutrons**.

prompt: Finish the aluminium example. An aluminium atom has 13 protons and 14 neutrons. How many electrons does it have?
explain: 13. An atom has no overall charge, so its electrons equal its protons. 27, the mass number, is the classic slip: the mass number counts no electrons at all.

md:
Electrons fill **shells** from the inside out. For the first 20 elements the first shell holds up to **2**, the second up to **8**, the third up to **8**, and anything left starts the **fourth**.
The **electronic configuration** lists the shells from the inside, separated by commas: sodium's 11 electrons are **2,8,1**; calcium's 20 are **2,8,8,2**. The numbers always add up to the number of electrons.

title: Why the arrangement matters
md: The electrons in the **outer shell** decide how an atom reacts. Elements with the same number of outer electrons behave alike, which is why they share a group of the Periodic Table, and why the lessons on ions and bonding start from the outer shell.

title: GCSE Chemistry - Electronic Structure (2027/28 exams)
why: A second run through filling shells and drawing configurations. Cognito calls it electronic structure; CCEA's word is electronic configuration.

prompt: Write the electronic configuration of a potassium atom, atomic number 19.
explain: 2,8,8,1. The third shell stops at 8 for these elements, so the nineteenth electron starts the fourth shell. 2,8,9 is the slip to avoid.

md:
An **ion** is a charged particle made when an atom **gains or loses electrons**. The protons never change, so the charge is **protons minus electrons**.
Oxygen has 8 protons. Gaining 2 electrons gives it 10, so the charge is 8 − 10 = −2, written 2−: the oxide ion, $\ce{O^{2-}}$, configuration **2,8**. Magnesium has 12 protons; losing 2 electrons leaves 10, a charge of 2+: $\ce{Mg^{2+}}$, also **2,8**.
Work out an ion's configuration from its **electrons**, never from its atomic number.

prompt: A sulfur atom, atomic number 16, gains 2 electrons to become the sulfide ion, S²⁻. How many electrons does the sulfide ion have?
explain: 16 + 2 = 18. A negative ion has gained electrons, so add them. Its configuration is then 2,8,8.

md:
Atoms of different elements can join by chemical bonds. The result is a **compound**: **two or more elements chemically combined**. Magnesium oxide is magnesium and oxygen chemically combined.
Each part of that definition carries weight: say **elements**, not atoms; say **two or more**, not 'several'; and say **chemically** combined, because a mixture is not.

prompt: Which of these is the definition of a compound?
options: two or more elements chemically combined
two or more atoms joined together
two or more elements mixed together
answer: two or more elements chemically combined
explain: Elements, two or more, chemically combined. 'Atoms' would also fit a molecule of a single element, such as oxygen, and 'mixed' describes a mixture.

define **atomic number** (protons only) and **mass number** (protons and neutrons).
work out the protons, neutrons and electrons in any atom or ion from its numbers.
write the electronic configuration of any atom or ion up to calcium, **2,8,8,2**.
define a **compound**: two or more elements chemically combined.

Atomic structure sits near the start of most C1 papers, usually Question 1 or 2: a particle table, a definition and a configuration. The first mark is often a definition; the last is usually an ion's configuration or charge. Stuck on an ion? Start from the protons, which never change, then add or take away electrons.
